claim: Overalls is listed as BrE among bipartite plural-only nouns. For the garment covering both parts of the body, the text says AmE has singular overall.
evidence_summary: OED overall, n. (revised 2004): sense 1, the singular protective garment, is chiefly British. Senses 2b–c, chiefly in plural, cover protective trousers, bib-and-strap trousers and later a boiler suit; 2b is originally and chiefly U.S., and 2c has U.S. quotations (Sears, Roebuck, 1897). Wiktionary agrees.
finding: American English uses plural overalls for a garment covering legs and chest, and the OED records no American singular. The BrE label in [26i] is too narrow, and “AmE here has singular overall” reverses the evidence.
inference: Is overalls restricted to BrE, and does AmE use singular overall for this garment?

evidence.passage: §3.2.1, p. 341 [26i] and following paragraph. “BrE overalls, however, denotes a garment covering both parts of the body; AmE here has singular overall”.
evidence.example: Wiktionary entries for overalls and overall, read as wikitext through the MediaWiki API.
evidence.establishes: The variety labels conflict with a dictionary source. Edited dictionaries returned HTTP 403 to the audit tools.
evidence.note: Local source (working note, unpublished draft or local copy); not online.

evidence.example: overalls: “(US, Canada, Australia) Loose-fitting pants with supporting cross-straps and a panel of material in the chest (called a bib)”. overall, noun: “(British) A garment worn over other clothing to protect it; a coverall or boiler suit.” and “(in the plural, US) A garment, worn for manual labor, with an integral covering extending to the chest”.
evidence.establishes: A collaborative dictionary that assigns plural overalls to US usage and singular overall to British usage.

evidence.example: Sense 1, a protective outer garment, labelled chiefly British. Sense 2, chiefly in plural, protective trousers: 2b “Originally and chiefly U.S.”; 2c bib-and-strap trousers, later also a boiler suit, quoted from Sears, Roebuck (1897) and the New York Times Magazine (1990).
evidence.establishes: The singular is the British form. American usage has the plural for garments covering the legs and chest.
evidence.locator: Meaning & use, senses 1, 2b, 2c. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.
